planting.note: Plant in spring or early fall; dormant foliage dies back fully in winter.

directions: Divide fans every 3-4 years in spring to keep bloom counts high, and deadhead spent blooms daily during the midseason flush for tidier scapes. Bred by Patricia R. Cochenour, this red spider with a bright yellow throat carries a 4:1+ petal ratio and claimed the American Hemerocallis Society's Harris Olson Spider Award in 2025. Water deeply at the base rather than overhead to protect the narrow, twisting petals from splash damage.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Semi-evergreen; in cold zones mulch crowns the first winter after fall planting.

directions: A heavy 30-bud, 5-branch scape means this cultivar benefits from staking in windy sites and a mid-season high-phosphorus feeding to sustain the long rebloom. Registered by Scott Elliott in 2016, its lavender-orange blend with a chevron-shaped dark pink band and extended green-yellow throat earned the AHS Harris Olson Spider Award in 2023. Its 4.9:1 petal ratio gives it an especially pronounced, twisted spider silhouette.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Evergreen foliage in mild climates; mulch crowns where winters dip below zone 6.

directions: Give this black-self spider afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the velvety near-black petals from bleaching; it is naturally sun-resistant but benefits from relief in zone 8-9 summers. Patrick Stamile bred it in 2007, and it took the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2016. Its tetraploid vigor supports a long early-midseason rebloom cycle on 38-inch scapes.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Semi-evergreen; divide congested clumps every 3-4 years for best bud count.

directions: The near-black purple self deepens in cooler morning light, so plant where it gets direct early sun to show its darkest color before afternoon heat fades it slightly. Hybridized by Ned Roberts and registered in 2005, it is a diploid spider variant with a 4-5:1 petal ratio that won the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2015. Keep soil evenly moist through midseason bloom to prevent bud blast on its nocturnal-opening flowers.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Tall scapes benefit from a sheltered spot away from strong wind.

directions: At 44 inches tall with 45-bud scapes, this cultivar makes a dramatic back-of-border spider and benefits from a spring top-dressing of compost to fuel its heavy bud count. Patrick Stamile registered it in 2002; its black-violet blend over a green throat carries a light fragrance and earned the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2010. Its tetraploid, evergreen habit supports reliable midseason rebloom in warm-winter gardens.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Evergreen foliage; in cold zones protect crowns with mulch over winter.

directions: The silvery watermark over lavender petals shows best in morning sun with some afternoon relief in hot regions, since strong heat can flatten the watercolor contrast. Patrick Stamile bred this fragrant, tetraploid spider in 2002, and it took the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2009. It reblooms reliably through midseason when kept consistently watered and fed lightly after the first flush.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Divide every 3-4 years to maintain the heavy 5-way branching and bud count.

directions: This pink spider with a darker pink eye above a large green throat is part of Katisue Herrington's long-running Oz-themed introductions; registered in 2001, it first earned an Honorable Mention before the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2008. Give it full sun and consistent moisture through its 30-bud bloom cycle for best eye-zone contrast. Avoid overhead watering late in the day to reduce petal spotting on its wide, extended throat.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Semi-evergreen; mulch crowns in colder zones over winter.

directions: With an 11-inch bloom on 44-inch scapes, this red-self spider needs rich, well-drained soil to support its oversized flowers without flopping. Dan and Jane Trimmer registered it in 2003, and its clean red-on-green coloring earned the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2008. Tetraploid vigor gives it dependable early-midseason rebloom when deadheaded regularly.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Dormant foliage; divide congested clumps every 3-4 years.

directions: Its tall, willowy scapes earn the cultivar name, so site it toward the back of a border where its red self blooms with a yellow-green throat can catch full sun without shading shorter neighbors. Bred by the Trimmers and registered in 1996, it won the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2007. Deadhead faded blooms daily since the flowers are naturally self-cleaning but look tidiest with help.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Divide every 3-4 years to sustain bloom count on this older but still vigorous cultivar.

directions: A compact spider at just under 3 feet, it suits mid-border placement where the red petals and lime-green throat read clearly against darker foliage neighbors. Registered by Dorothy Warrell in 1988, it collected an Award of Merit before the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2006. It performs reliably in both cold and warm zones thanks to its adaptable, long-blooming nature.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Evergreen foliage; benefits from winter mulch outside zone 6.

directions: One of the earliest-blooming large spiders available, this red self with a green throat opens its 9.5-inch flowers on 46-inch scapes well before most other spiders in the garden. Patrick Stamile registered it in 1997, and it won the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2003, praised as an outstanding early spider. Its evergreen, tetraploid habit supports a dependable rebloom cycle when watered consistently through the season.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Compact habit suits front-of-border planting; divide every 3-4 years.

directions: The twisted, cinnamon-chevroned petals on a yellow ground are lightly fragrant, so plant it near a path or patio where its scent can be enjoyed. Clarence Crochet registered it in 1997, and its exceptionally high 5.2:1 petal ratio helped it win the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2002; it also carries the RHS Award of Garden Merit. Full sun keeps the chevron markings crisp on its 8.5-inch blooms.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list

planting.note: Evergreen diploid; divide every 3-4 years for best flower count.

directions: A bright, clean yellow self spider with an extended bloom period, it works well massed near the front of a sunny bed where its compact 26-inch scapes won't be lost behind taller perennials. Bred by Inez Tarrant and registered in 1987, it won the Harris Olson Spider Award in 2001. Its evergreen, diploid habit benefits from winter protection in colder zones but otherwise asks for little beyond routine watering and occasional feeding.
sources: AHS Harris Olson Spider Award list
